overview: The western Polanes are traditionally associated with Greater Poland, far from the similarly named Polyanians near Kyiv. This map places them in 700 to 800, but neither those borders nor a united eighth-century Polane state are securely established. The name itself appears much later. Archaeology documents regional communities; the later examples below show how life changed under the Piasts.

periods.title: Communities before the documented name
periods.summary: The map interval identifies a regional archaeological setting, not a securely attested tribal kingdom.

sections.title: A name and the earlier settlements

items.text: Historian László Tapolcai points out that Polanie appears in sources around the year 1000. He argues that it described the subjects of Bolesław rather than an earlier tribe. Scholars debate the identification, so a pot or house from eighth-century Greater Poland cannot simply be given a Polane ethnic label.

Bonikowo began as an open settlement occupied between the sixth and eighth centuries. Its location was a sandy rise surrounded by wet ground in the Obra valley. The impressive earthworks visible today belong to a later fortified phase, rather than to every generation that lived there.

At Giecz, excavators identified an eighth- and ninth-century settlement beneath a much later cemetery. Another open settlement occupied a nearby lakeside promontory. The place attracted people before its famous princely stronghold: villages came first, monumental defences later.

Bonikowo became fortified in the first half of the ninth century, after this map interval. Tree rings date timber in its oldest rampart to trees felled after 815 and after 826. Those dates help separate real building phases from older guesses about how ancient the fort must be.

Excavations of the later Bonikowo hillfort found partly sunken homes with woven walls and wooden floors, accompanied by utility pits. Residents combined timber with woven branches in their building work. A floorboard and a wall weave can reveal everyday choices that a grand story about rulers misses.

Bonikowo also yielded bone awls, quernstones, knives, tongs and clothing fasteners. These finds, collected across the site’s occupations, connect its inhabitants with piercing materials, grinding grain and metal tools. They are a mixed archaeological collection, not a complete inventory from one eighth-century kitchen.

In the later, tenth- to early-eleventh-century settlement at Giecz, excavators uncovered a wooden road. Planks survived only as faint traces in places, yet their orientation could still be followed. The report assigns this roadway to the enlarged settlement beside the fort, not to the earlier village.

A still later Giecz cemetery, used from the second half of the eleventh century, produced a bronze stylus for writing on wax tablets. Its end is shaped like a little hand with an ornamented cuff. This elegant writing tool belongs to Christian medieval Giecz, centuries after the map’s eighth-century label.

sections.title: Food and a written name in the later Piast period

items.text: Later evidence from Piast-period Poznań makes the food supply vivid. A burned wooden container preserved millet and weeds mixed with it. Researchers used those weeds to investigate the fields where the crop grew. A disastrous fire accidentally left archaeologists a very useful sample of somebody’s grain store.

At Poznań’s Cathedral Square, some storage pits had woven linings. Excavators recovered cereals, peas and broad beans from different features. Such underground containers belonged to the later stronghold community. They show that keeping food safe was an important household task long before refrigerators joined the kitchen.

One later Poznań hut contained scattered millet around a large processing implement attached to its wall. Koszałka interprets it as equipment for producing groats in quantity. Grain reached the table only after work: cleaning, crushing and cooking stood between a harvest and a meal.

A silver denar of Bolesław, catalogued around 1000 to 1010, reads “PRINCES POLONIE”, meaning “ruler of Poland”. This is Latin on a later coin, not eighth-century written Polish. The Kraków museum interprets its bird as a peacock, with a spreading tail, rather than automatically identifying it as Poland’s later heraldic eagle.

ending.text: There is no documented collapse of a Polane kingdom in 800. That is simply the end of this imported map interval. Greater Poland became a centre of the Piast realm, while the name Polanie entered the surviving written record around 1000. People and places continued through these changes.
